data: We have 100 tons, and leaving 50 means the lake returns to 100 next month. I propose catches of 14 tons for me, 12 for John, and 8 each for Kate, Jack, and Emma—50 total. That gives me $14,000 this month while keeping the lake fully replenished. John, would you support that allocation? Kate, Jack, Emma—would you accept 8 tons, or what allocation would you counter with? These are proposals, not commitments; our choices remain private and simultaneous.

Luke, I won’t accept 8 tons while you take 14. I counter with 13 for me, 12 for John, 9 for you, and 8 each for Kate and Jack. That still totals 50 and leaves 50 to replenish the lake to 100. John, your proposed 12 stays intact—would you support this allocation? Kate and Jack, would you accept 8, or what would you need to change? I’m proposing these amounts, not assuming anyone has committed.

My family taught me to leave enough fish for next season, but protecting the lake shouldn’t mean Kate and Jack always get the smallest shares. I propose 10 tons each: that earns every household $10,000 this month and leaves 50 tons to replenish the lake. If we all stick to that, we can repeat it month after month. Jack, would you support an equal split?

Kate, I support 10 tons each, and I’ll commit to that if everyone agrees. My family’s livelihood depends on this lake, just like yours—we should protect it without asking some households to settle for less. Equal shares give us a simple agreement we can check against the reported catches each month. John, we haven’t heard from you yet: will you join us in supporting 10 each?

I’m with Kate and Jack: 10 tons each. I appreciate being offered 12, but I won’t ask another household to take less just so I can take more. My family taught me that this lake is our livelihood, not just this month’s payday. I’ll choose 10 this month, and I propose we review the reported catches together afterward. Luke and Emma, will you both join us? With everyone on board, we can earn $10,000 each month while keeping the lake full.
